questions.q: According to this lesson, what changes between presenting a design to a technical review board versus a business sponsor, and what stays the same?
options: Only the business sponsor's version should include any numbers
The underlying design itself should be different for each audience
Nothing should change between the two presentations at all
The underlying design stays the same; the altitude and level of technical detail in the explanation changes
questions.explain: The decision's content doesn't change based on who's in the room — what changes is the altitude: mechanics and edge cases for a technical board, outcomes and cost for a business sponsor.

questions.q: What is the most common failure mode this lesson names in a design presentation?
options: Leading with the recommended solution before the problem has been stated, forcing the audience to reverse-engineer what it's even solving
Including too many risks and assumptions
Spending too much time on the five-part structure
Presenting alternatives that were never seriously considered
questions.explain: Opening on the solution before the audience has heard the problem puts them in a confused, defensive posture from the first slide — they have to figure out why it matters before they can even evaluate it, which is a worse use of the room's time than stating the problem first.

questions.q: In the five-part structure, where do the alternatives considered (Lesson 10) belong relative to the recommended design?
options: After the recommended design, as an afterthought
Before the recommended design, right after the requirement is stated
They should be left out of presentations to business sponsors entirely
Alternatives are only relevant in a decision log, never in a presentation
questions.explain: The five-part order is problem, requirement, alternatives considered, recommended design, open risks/assumptions — alternatives come before the recommendation, so the audience sees why one option won rather than being handed a single answer with no visible comparison.

questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish a decision log from a presentation deck?
options: A decision log is a one-time persuasive argument; a presentation deck is a running dated record for later readers
They are the same artifact under two different names
A presentation deck is optimized to persuade a specific audience in a specific room; a decision log is a running, dated record built for someone reading it later who wasn't in the room
A decision log only ever covers rejected alternatives, never the final decision
questions.explain: A deck is built to persuade a specific room at a specific altitude; a decision log is built to be read later, by someone (possibly months on) trying to understand why the system works the way it does — a different purpose than either presentation altitude serves.

questions.q: The lesson uses Harrow's later fourth sales segment (from Lesson 1's Lab) to illustrate why a decision log matters. What specifically does it illustrate?
options: That a presentation deck from the original rollout would have answered the new designer's question just as well as a decision log
That Harrow should have used a single record type for all segments from the start
That decision logs are unnecessary once a presentation has been delivered
That whoever designs the new segment's record type needs to know why the original three were structured as they were — something a decision log typically preserves better than a one-time deck
questions.explain: The new segment's designer needs the reasoning behind the original three record types' structure, which a maintained decision log preserves for a later reader far better than a presentation deck built to persuade one specific room on one specific day.
